problem: The division is written as '544 × 10⁶ ÷ 34 × 10⁶'. Read left to right by normal precedence this multiplies back by 10⁶ and gives a nonsense answer (1.6 × 10¹⁰); the powers of ten must be grouped or cancelled before the numbers are divided.

'A VLAN is a logical LAN carved inside one switch' is too narrow. A VLAN is a logical grouping of ports that normally spans several switches joined by trunk links, which is exactly why one building can be split into several LANs.
fix: A VLAN is a logical LAN created by grouping switch ports, usually across several switches joined by trunk links, so one building can behave as several separate LANs.

where: Section 1 last paragraph, Exam trap 1, Quiz Q8 answer
problem: The invented term 'private WAN-style link' for a 40 km or 25 km fibre inside one company conflicts with the chapter's own span table (MAN is roughly 5–50 km) and leaves students unsure what to call such a link. Q8's answer only labels the rented case as a MAN.
fix: Say plainly: a 25–40 km link between one company's own buildings in one city is a private MAN (the company is its own provider); it becomes a WAN only when it leaves the city or crosses a carrier's long-distance network. Keep the point that span alone does not decide.

problem: 'Divide by 8 the wrong way and you are off by 64' is hard to follow. Converting MB to Mbit means multiplying by 8; a student who divides instead is off by a factor of 64, but the sentence does not say which operation is the wrong one.
fix: To go from MB to Mbit multiply by 8, never divide. Dividing instead of multiplying puts you off by a factor of 64 (8 × 8).

problem: The caption says the figure shows LAN as 'the one network a single organisation owns' and that ownership passes from one organisation to many as you move right. Exam trap 4 and Section 1 both say a company can own its own city-wide links, so the caption overstates the rule.
fix: Say that ownership usually moves from a single organisation at the LAN end to several carriers at the WAN and Internet ends, but a company can still own a private MAN or private long-distance links.
